/supplements/msm.title: MSM for joint pain: evidence and safety | Living With Arthritis
/supplements/msm.description: MSM evidence is limited. Read about uncertainty, safety and why supplements should not replace recommended osteoarthritis treatment.
/supplements/msm.question: MSM for joint pain: evidence and safety
/supplements/msm.answer: MSM is a supplement sold for joint pain. Small, short studies suggest possible benefit, but they do not establish reliable long-term benefit or safety. NICE NG226 does not include a recommendation on MSM. It advises against offering glucosamine. Do not replace prescribed treatment with either supplement.
/supplements/msm.bodyHtml:
What the evidence can tell us

Arthritis UK describes a small number of short MSM trials, including one study of MSM with glucosamine. This does not establish that the combination is better for everyone, or that MSM is a proven arthritis treatment. NICE NG226 recommends tailored therapeutic exercise and weight management where appropriate. It does not include a recommendation to offer MSM.

No recommended arthritis dose

We do not recommend an MSM dose, product or trial course for arthritis. Research doses vary and should not be treated as personal dosing advice. Ask a pharmacist or your GP before starting any supplement.

Safety and other treatment

Short studies cannot establish long-term safety. Tell a pharmacist about your medicines, health conditions, allergies and any supplements you already use. Seek advice before use during pregnancy or breastfeeding. A supplement should not delay assessment or replace exercise, prescribed medicines or other treatment agreed with your healthcare team.

Keep recommended care in place

For osteoarthritis, NICE recommends exercise tailored to your needs and weight management where appropriate. Discuss suitable pain relief with a pharmacist or clinician. Supplements do not replace treatment agreed with your healthcare team.

Planning your next step

Write down what is hardest for you, such as walking, stairs, sleep or daily tasks, and what you would like to improve. Bring your questions to a healthcare appointment. A useful plan considers your needs and preferences rather than promising the same result for everyone.

For osteoarthritis, NICE recommends therapeutic exercise tailored to your needs. Local muscle strengthening and aerobic activity can be part of this. Ask whether supervised exercise would help you get started. Exercise may initially increase pain, but regular, consistent exercise can improve pain and function over time.

If you are living with overweight or obesity, ask about suitable weight-management support. This is different from recommending weight loss to everyone. If you are losing weight unintentionally or have difficulty eating, ask your GP for an assessment instead. Keep prescribed treatment in place while discussing changes with your healthcare team.

/supplements/glucosamine.question: Glucosamine for arthritis: NICE advice and safety
/supplements/glucosamine.answer: NICE advises healthcare professionals not to offer glucosamine for osteoarthritis because there is no strong evidence of benefit. Some trials report improvements, but results are inconsistent. We do not recommend glucosamine as an arthritis treatment or a substitute for exercise, weight management where appropriate, or prescribed treatment.

NICE advice and research uncertainty

NICE NG226 recommendations 1.4.6 and 1.4.7 advise against offering glucosamine for osteoarthritis and say there is no strong evidence of benefit. Arthritis UK describes mixed trial results and uncertain, generally modest benefits. Its information is more permissive than NICE in places. This website follows NICE's recommendation rather than suggesting a trial course or a preferred formulation.

No treatment dose recommended here

We do not recommend a glucosamine dose or product for arthritis. Trial doses are not personal dosing advice. If you already take it or are thinking about it, ask a pharmacist or your GP about safety and interactions. Do not stop prescribed treatment to try a supplement.

Safety questions

Glucosamine can cause stomach upset and other side effects. Some products are made from shellfish. Ask a pharmacist or GP before use if you have diabetes, take warfarin or other medicines, have an allergy, or are pregnant or breastfeeding. Tell your healthcare team about all supplements you take.

/supplements/turmeric.title: Turmeric and curcumin for arthritis: uncertainty and safety | Living With Arthritis
/supplements/turmeric.description: Turmeric and curcumin are not proven replacements for arthritis medicines. Read about uncertain benefits, dosing and interactions.
/supplements/turmeric.question: Turmeric and curcumin for arthritis: uncertainty and safety
/supplements/turmeric.answer: Some small studies suggest turmeric or curcumin may help arthritis symptoms, but the evidence does not establish a reliable benefit, an effective dose or equivalence to anti-inflammatory medicines. NICE NG226 does not include a recommendation on turmeric. Do not replace prescribed medicines with a supplement. Ask a pharmacist about interactions.
/supplements/turmeric.bodyHtml:
What is known and what remains uncertain

Curcumin is a component of turmeric. Products and study methods vary, making results difficult to compare. Arthritis UK's 2026 dietitian advice says trials are too few and small to establish whether it works or how much to take. Other Arthritis UK pages discuss possible modest benefits. These differences are a reason for caution, not a basis for promising an effect.

No recommended arthritis dose

We do not recommend a curcumin dose, brand, enhanced-absorption product or trial course for arthritis. A dose used in a study is not a dose recommendation for you. Do not assume a supplement matches ibuprofen or diclofenac, is safer than these medicines, or needs black pepper to work.

Safety and medicines

Supplements can cause side effects and interact with medicines. Speak to a pharmacist or GP before use, especially if you take blood thinners or medicines for diabetes, cancer or immune suppression. Do not replace prescribed treatment. Turmeric used as a cooking ingredient is not the same as a concentrated supplement.

/faq/arthritis-and-nutrition.question: What nutrients help with arthritis?

/faq/arthritis-and-nutrition.bodyHtml:
Food and osteoarthritis care

NICE identifies tailored exercise and weight management, where appropriate, as core osteoarthritis treatments. There is no single food or supplement that should replace this care or prescribed treatment.

Avoid treatment promises

We do not recommend glucosamine, MSM or curcumin as proven arthritis treatments or give a supplement dose for pain relief. NICE advises against offering glucosamine for osteoarthritis because there is no strong evidence of benefit. Other supplements are not established substitutes for recommended care.

Individual nutrition needs

Ask your GP or a dietitian about unintentional weight loss, poor appetite or a restricted diet. A supplement may be advised for a specific nutritional need, but correcting a deficiency is different from treating arthritis. Ask a pharmacist about interactions before starting any supplement.

/faq/arthritis-exercise-myths.description: Exercise and osteoarthritis: NICE advice on tailored strengthening, aerobic activity, building up gradually and getting help with your plan.
/faq/arthritis-exercise-myths.question: What are common myths about exercise and arthritis?
/faq/arthritis-exercise-myths.answer: NICE recommends exercise tailored to your needs for osteoarthritis, including local muscle strengthening and aerobic activity. Regular exercise can help pain and function. Start at a manageable level and ask a physiotherapist if you are unsure what is suitable.
/faq/arthritis-exercise-myths.bodyHtml:
Exercise is part of osteoarthritis treatment

NICE recommends tailored therapeutic exercise for everyone with osteoarthritis. This can include local muscle strengthening and general aerobic activity. The plan should reflect your needs and preferences.

Build up gradually

Joint pain may initially increase when starting exercise. NICE advises that regular, consistent exercise can reduce pain and improve function and quality of life in the long term. Ask about supervised exercise if you need help getting started.

Do not use a fixed pain or medicine rule

There is no single exercise dose or pain threshold that suits everyone. Ask a physiotherapist about adapting activity if symptoms are difficult to manage. Do not take a medicine specifically before exercise without checking that it is suitable for you.

/faq/reduce-arthritis-pain-naturally.question: How can I reduce arthritis pain naturally?

/faq/reduce-arthritis-pain-naturally.bodyHtml:

NICE recommends local muscle strengthening and aerobic activity for osteoarthritis. Start at a level you can manage. Some discomfort at first is possible; ask a physiotherapist for advice if you are unsure what is suitable.

Weight management where appropriate

If you have osteoarthritis and are living with overweight or obesity, supported weight loss can reduce pain and improve function. It is not appropriate for everyone, particularly if you are underweight, losing weight unintentionally or at risk of malnutrition.

Keep necessary treatment

Self-management can sit alongside medicines and other treatment. Do not stop prescribed medicines or replace inflammatory-arthritis treatment with food, supplements or home remedies. Ask a pharmacist or your healthcare team about persistent pain.

/guides/frailty-management-hub.title: Frailty & Arthritis Guide | Living With Arthritis
/guides/frailty-management-hub.description: Frailty and arthritis: why individual assessment matters, how to ask about activity and nutrition support, and when to contact your GP.
/guides/frailty-management-hub.bodyHtml:
Editorial safety update: 24 November 2026. This updated information is awaiting a separate clinical review.

1. What is frailty and how does it connect to arthritis?

Frailty is a clinical syndrome of reduced reserve across multiple body systems — muscle, bone, balance, cognition and immunity. Adults with arthritis are at higher risk because chronic pain reduces activity, accelerating muscle loss (sarcopenia) and balance decline.

A clinician can assess frailty alongside your other health conditions, medicines, daily activities and priorities.

2. The five pillars of frailty prevention

  • Strength: progressive resistance training 2–3 times per week.
  • Nutrition: individual nutrition assessment if appetite is poor or weight loss is unintentional.
  • Cognition: regular mental stimulation, reading, puzzles, learning.
  • Mood: identify and treat depression and anxiety early.
  • Social connection: ask about loneliness and support that matters to the person.

3. Exercise for frailty: safe progressions

Ask a physiotherapist about activity suited to your strength, balance and health conditions. Seated or supported exercises may be appropriate. Do not attempt unsupported balance exercises if you are at risk of falling.

See our exercise hub for progressions.

4. Nutrition strategies for muscle preservation

If you have poor appetite, difficulty eating or unintentional weight loss, ask your GP about nutrition assessment and dietitian support. Any supplements or protein targets should reflect your needs and health conditions.

Read our diet hub and foods to avoid with arthritis.

5. When to ask for help: red flags and support services

  • Unintentional weight loss greater than 5% in 12 months
  • More than one fall in 12 months
  • New or worsening exhaustion most days
  • Struggling with dressing, washing or shopping
  • Slower walking pace (under 0.8 m/s)

Speak to your GP, who can refer to community physiotherapy, falls clinics and social prescribing.

6. What families are looking for

Many adult children begin researching frailty after a parent has a fall, loses weight or struggles with day-to-day tasks. Support should be tailored to the person and may involve activity, nutrition, home safety and practical help.

Your GP can advise on assessment and suitable local support. The plan should reflect the person's needs and preferences.

Common frailty solutions

  • Nutrition support if assessment identifies a need
  • Supplements only when suitable for an identified need
  • Medical alert systems, personal alarms and fall detectors
  • Home modifications — grab rails, ramps, improved lighting, removing trip hazards
  • Geriatric assessments (Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment) and frailty case management
  • Balance, resistance and tai chi programmes — group or one-to-one

Educational information only — we don't endorse specific brands or providers. Speak to your GP, community physiotherapy or social services for personalised recommendations.

Source: NICE NG56 recommendations on multimorbidity and frailty assessment.

Related guides

  • Sarcopenia & muscle loss
  • Fall prevention for older adults
  • Bone density & osteoporosis
  • Osteoarthritis guide

Frequently asked questions

What is frailty?

Frailty is a clinical state of reduced reserve and resilience across multiple body systems, leaving older adults more vulnerable to falls, hospital admission and slower recovery.

Does arthritis cause frailty?

Arthritis does not directly cause frailty, but pain, inflammation and inactivity accelerate muscle loss and reduce function — pushing people into pre-frail or frail states earlier.

Can frailty be reversed?

Frailty needs an individual assessment and care plan. Exercise, nutrition support and treatment review may help maintain function, but improvement varies and reversal cannot be promised.

How is frailty measured?

Clinicians use tools such as the Clinical Frailty Scale, gait speed (<0.8 m/s), grip strength and the Fried phenotype (weakness, slowness, exhaustion, low activity, weight loss).

What exercise is safest for frail older adults?

Supervised seated strength work, sit-to-stand repetitions, resistance bands and balance drills — progressed gradually. Avoid high-impact loading until strength returns.

When should I ask for help?

Speak to your GP if you notice unintentional weight loss, more than one fall in 12 months, exhaustion, or struggling with daily tasks like dressing or shopping.
/guides/frailty-management-hub.answer: Frailty needs an individual assessment and care plan. Support may include tailored activity, nutrition advice and treatment review. Improvement varies and reversal cannot be promised.

/guides/knee-replacement-surgery.title: Knee Replacement Surgery UK — Guide | Living With Arthritis
/guides/knee-replacement-surgery.description: UK patient guide to knee replacement: when to consider it, prehab, hospital stay, recovery timeline, exercises, risks and waiting-list options.
/guides/knee-replacement-surgery.bodyHtml:
A Patient's Guide to Knee Replacement Surgery

Knee replacement — known clinically as knee arthroplasty — is one of the most successful and well-studied operations performed in the UK. Around 110,000 knee replacements are carried out each year in England, Wales and Northern Ireland (National Joint Registry, 2023), and the great majority of patients report substantial pain relief and improved mobility within a year of surgery.

This guide walks you through every stage of the patient journey: deciding whether surgery is right for you, what to expect in hospital, how to prepare your home, and the realities of recovery. It is written for UK patients and reflects current NICE guidance (NG226) and Royal College of Surgeons standards.

When to Consider Knee Replacement

Knee replacement is recommended when conservative treatments no longer control pain and disability. Typical triggers include:

  • Pain that disturbs sleep — waking at night or being unable to find a comfortable position
  • Walking difficulties that affect your quality of life, with no minimum walking-time threshold required
  • Difficulty with stairs, getting out of a chair, or driving
  • Persistent stiffness and visible deformity (bow-leg or knock-knee)
  • X-ray evidence of advanced arthritis — narrowed joint space, bone spurs, bone-on-bone contact
  • Non-surgical treatment is ineffective or unsuitable

If these apply, ask your GP for an orthopaedic referral. You may also want to read our companion guide on knee arthritis and managing the wait for surgery.

Types of Knee Replacement

Total Knee Replacement (TKR)

The whole joint surface is replaced — the lower end of the femur, the top of the tibia, and usually the underside of the patella. TKR accounts for around 90% of UK knee replacements. Implants are typically cobalt-chromium and polyethylene, fixed with bone cement.

Partial (Unicompartmental) Knee Replacement

Only the damaged compartment (usually the inner side) is resurfaced. Recovery is faster and the knee feels more "natural", but it suits only around 1 in 4 patients — those with arthritis confined to one compartment and intact ligaments.

Patellofemoral Replacement

Resurfaces only the kneecap and its groove. Used for isolated kneecap arthritis — about 1–2% of cases.

Revision Knee Replacement

A second operation if the original implant loosens, wears out or becomes infected. Revisions are technically harder, take longer to recover from, and are best done in specialist centres.

Preparing for Surgery (Prehabilitation)

"Prehab" — getting fitter before surgery — has strong evidence for shorter hospital stays and faster recovery. UK enhanced recovery programmes recommend:

  • Quadriceps and glute strengthening — straight-leg raises, mini-squats, step-ups (3–4 sessions per week for 6+ weeks)
  • Aerobic conditioning — cycling, swimming, or aqua-walking
  • Weight loss — a BMI under 35 reduces complication risk; many trusts now require BMI optimisation
  • Stopping smoking at least 8 weeks before surgery — smoking doubles wound infection risk
  • Reducing alcohol to under 14 units per week
  • Optimising chronic conditions — diabetes (HbA1c < 69 mmol/mol), blood pressure, anaemia
  • Dental check-up — untreated dental infection is a known source of implant infection

You will usually attend a pre-operative assessment clinic 2–6 weeks before surgery for blood tests, ECG, MRSA swabs, and an anaesthetic review.

Preparing Your Home

A small amount of planning makes early recovery far easier:

  • Move frequently used items to waist height — no bending or reaching
  • Set up a recovery base downstairs if possible, with a firm chair (knee at 90°), footstool, and bedside table
  • Remove trip hazards — loose rugs, trailing cables, clutter on stairs
  • Buy or borrow a raised toilet seat, long-handled shoe horn, sock aid, grabber and shower stool
  • Batch-cook and freeze meals for the first 2–3 weeks
  • Arrange help with shopping, pets, laundry and childcare for at least 2 weeks
  • Tell family you will not be driving for around 6 weeks

What Happens in Hospital

Most UK hospital trusts now follow an enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) pathway. A typical timeline:

Day of Surgery

You arrive fasted (usually from midnight, or as instructed). Anaesthetic is most often spinal with sedation, which is associated with less blood loss and quicker recovery than general anaesthesia. Surgery takes 60–90 minutes. You are encouraged to stand and walk within a few hours with a physiotherapist.

Days 1–2

Pain is managed with regular paracetamol, an anti-inflammatory if suitable, and short-term opioids. You will practise walking with crutches or a frame, climbing stairs, and bending the knee. Most patients are discharged within 1–3 days, some on the same day under modern ERAS protocols.

Before Discharge

You will be given blood-thinning injections or tablets for 2–4 weeks to reduce clot risk, a clear exercise sheet, contact numbers, and a follow-up appointment for around 6 weeks.

Recovery Timeline: Week by Week

Recovery is gradual. The pattern below is typical but individual — your surgical team's advice always takes priority.

Weeks 1–2: Pain & Swelling Control

  • Walk short distances with crutches every 1–2 hours
  • Ice the knee for 15–20 minutes, 4–6 times daily
  • Elevate the leg above heart level when resting
  • Do the prescribed exercises 3–4 times daily — quad sets, ankle pumps, heel slides
  • Aim for knee bend (flexion) of 70–90° by the end of week 2

Weeks 3–6: Building Movement

  • Progress to one crutch, then walking unaided indoors
  • Target flexion of 100–110° and full extension (straight knee)
  • Begin stationary cycling on low resistance once you have 100° of bend
  • 6-week orthopaedic review — surgeon checks wound, range of movement and X-rays
  • Most patients can return to driving once they can do an emergency stop comfortably (typically 6 weeks for a right knee)

Weeks 6–12: Strength & Confidence

  • Return to desk-based work, light shopping, social activities
  • Add resistance training, swimming, and longer walks
  • Swelling around the knee is normal for several more months

Months 3–12: Long-Term Recovery

  • Steady improvement in pain, strength and stamina
  • Return to recommended activities: walking, cycling, swimming, golf, doubles tennis, gentle hiking
  • Avoid high-impact activities — running, contact sport, jumping — which shorten implant life
  • Full recovery is usually reached between 6 and 12 months

Essential Recovery Exercises

These exercises should be done daily from day 1 unless your physiotherapist advises otherwise. See our full exercise hub for more progressions.

  • Quad sets — tighten the thigh muscle and push the back of the knee into the bed for 5 seconds, 10 reps
  • Ankle pumps — move feet up and down to reduce clot risk, 20 reps every hour
  • Heel slides — slide the heel towards the buttock to bend the knee, 10 reps
  • Straight-leg raise — with knee locked straight, lift the leg 20 cm, hold 5 seconds, 10 reps
  • Seated knee extension — sit on a firm chair, straighten the knee fully, hold 5 seconds, 10 reps
  • Standing knee bends — holding a worktop, bend the operated knee back behind you, 10 reps

Risks and How They Are Managed

Serious complications are uncommon but worth understanding. UK National Joint Registry data show:

  • Deep infection — around 1 in 100. Risk reduced by antibiotics at induction, laminar-flow theatres and good blood sugar control.
  • Blood clots (DVT / PE) — around 1 in 100 symptomatic, reduced by early mobilisation and post-op anticoagulants.
  • Stiffness requiring manipulation under anaesthetic — around 2–3%.
  • Nerve or blood-vessel injury — under 1%.
  • Persistent pain — 15–20% of patients report ongoing discomfort at 1 year; usually mild and manageable.
  • Implant loosening or wear — gradual; most implants last 20–25 years.
  • Death within 90 days — under 0.5%, mostly from cardiovascular events.

Risk is higher in patients who smoke, have a BMI above 40, or have poorly controlled diabetes, heart or kidney disease. Your surgical team will discuss your individual risk before consent.

Public Waiting Lists and Private Options

Knee replacement is a routine UK operation. Under the UK 18-week referral-to-treatment standard you have the right to be treated within 18 weeks of referral. If your local trust cannot meet this, you can ask to be transferred to another public or publicly funded independent provider — this is sometimes called the "right to choose".

Private knee replacement in the UK typically costs £12,000–£16,000 all-inclusive. Patients often choose private care to shorten waits or to select a specific consultant. Outcomes are similar to public care when the same surgeon and implant are used. See our guide on managing the UK waiting list for practical steps while you wait.

Alternatives and Delaying Surgery

NICE recommends therapeutic exercise for people with osteoarthritis and weight management if they are living with overweight or obesity. Treatment should reflect your needs and preferences.

  • Exercise: tailored strengthening and aerobic activity. ESCAPE-pain is a six-week education and exercise programme for hip and knee osteoarthritis. It can help symptoms and function; benefits vary.
  • Weight management: supported weight loss, where appropriate, can help pain and function. It is not a requirement to reach a particular BMI before referral.
  • Pain relief: NICE recommends a topical NSAID for knee osteoarthritis. If this is unsuitable or ineffective, a clinician may consider an oral NSAID after assessing risks, with gastroprotection. Paracetamol and weak opioids are not routinely recommended.
  • Steroid injections: may be considered when other medicines are unsuitable or ineffective, or to support exercise. NICE describes short-term relief of 2 to 10 weeks.
  • Walking aids: may help lower-limb osteoarthritis. Ask about a suitable aid and how to use it.

NICE advises against offering glucosamine or intra-articular hyaluronan for osteoarthritis. Referral for joint replacement should be considered when symptoms substantially affect quality of life and non-surgical management is ineffective or unsuitable. Do not delay asking for a referral because you have not completed an arbitrary exercise period.

Sources: NICE NG226 recommendations; Arthritis UK: ESCAPE-pain.

The Emotional Side of Surgery

Major surgery can be daunting. Anxiety, low mood and sleep disturbance are common before and after the operation. Patients often describe a "third-week dip" when the initial momentum fades and progress feels slow. This is normal. Recovery is rarely linear. Things that help:

  • Setting small weekly goals — bending 5° more, walking 5 minutes longer
  • Keeping a brief daily diary of pain, swelling and movement
  • Staying socially connected — visitors, video calls, the Living With Arthritis community
  • Speaking to your GP early if low mood persists beyond 2–3 weeks

Sources & Disclaimer

This guide draws on NICE guideline NG226 (Osteoarthritis in over 16s: diagnosis and management), the UK National Joint Registry 20th Annual Report (2023), Royal College of Surgeons of England commissioning guidance for knee replacement, British Orthopaedic Association enhanced recovery standards, and Cochrane reviews of prehabilitation and post-operative physiotherapy. It is for general education and does not replace personalised advice from your GP, surgeon or physiotherapist.

/symptom-checker.title: Arthritis symptom checker: educational guide finder | Living With Arthritis
/symptom-checker.description: Educational arthritis guide finder, not a diagnosis. NHS urgent and emergency advice, persistent joint swelling assessment and links to further reading.
/symptom-checker.question: Can this symptom checker diagnose arthritis?
/symptom-checker.answer: No. This tool only suggests educational guides and cannot diagnose arthritis or rule out an emergency. A hot swollen joint or sudden severe joint pain needs urgent GP assessment or NHS 111, even without fever. Go to A&E or call 999 for very bad joint pain after injury, inability to bear weight, or new bladder/bowel changes or saddle numbness with back pain. Call 999 for life-threatening symptoms.
/symptom-checker.bodyHtml:
When to get medical help

Ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 now for a hot swollen joint or sudden severe joint pain. Fever may be absent in joint infection. Do not wait for this checker to give a result.

Go to A&E or call 999 for very bad joint pain after a fall or injury, inability to walk or bear weight, a joint out of place, or numbness or tingling after injury. Do not drive yourself.

Back pain with new bladder or bowel changes, difficulty peeing, saddle numbness, sexual-function changes or symptoms in both legs needs emergency assessment. Go to A&E or call 999. Call 999 for life-threatening symptoms such as chest pain, severe breathlessness, collapse or stroke symptoms.

Persistent joint symptoms

See a GP when pain affects daily activities or sleep, swelling persists or keeps returning, symptoms have not improved after 2 weeks of home care, or morning stiffness lasts more than 30 minutes. Children with joint problems should see a GP.

Persistent soft swelling in small joints or several joints needs prompt assessment for possible inflammatory arthritis. NICE advises urgent specialist referral for suspected persistent synovitis involving small joints or more than one joint, even with normal blood tests. Tests should not delay referral.

What this checker does

Answers are used to rank related guides for education, not to diagnose a condition or calculate its probability. A safety screen comes first and later urgent answers interrupt the questionnaire. A result cannot rule out arthritis, infection or another condition. Ask a healthcare professional if you are worried.

The guides cover arthritis conditions, exercise, daily life, diet and benefits. They do not replace a healthcare appointment or a treatment plan. Do not stop prescribed medicines based on this tool. Your healthcare team can help assess symptoms and agree the next step with you.

/library/naproxen.title: Naproxen for Arthritis: Uses, Risks and Safety
/library/naproxen.description: Naproxen is an anti-inflammatory painkiller. Learn how it is used for arthritis, its main risks and when to ask a pharmacist or prescriber for advice.
/library/naproxen.question: Naproxen: uses and safety for arthritis
/library/naproxen.answer: Naproxen is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that can relieve pain and swelling in conditions including arthritis. It is not suitable for everyone and can cause stomach bleeding, kidney problems and other serious side effects. Ask a pharmacist or prescriber whether it is suitable for you.
/library/naproxen.bodyHtml:
What is Naproxen?

Naproxen is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID). It is used to relieve pain, reduce inflammation (swelling), and lower fever. Naproxen is commonly used for conditions such as arthritis, gout, menstrual pain, muscle aches, headaches, and back pain. Naproxen is prescribed for arthritis. Some UK pharmacy products have limited indications: Naprosyn Pain Relief 250 mg is for short-term muscle and joint pain in adults aged 18 to 50, for no more than 3 days; period-pain products have separate eligibility rules. Ask a pharmacist which product is suitable, and do not use a pharmacy product as ongoing arthritis treatment without medical advice.

How Does it Work?

Naproxen works by blocking the production of prostaglandins — chemicals in the body that trigger pain, inflammation, and fever. By reducing prostaglandin production, naproxen reduces pain and swelling at the site of injury or inflammation.

Common Uses

  • Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis
  • Gout attacks
  • Muscle and joint pain
  • Back pain
  • Menstrual (period) pain
  • Headaches and migraines
  • Ankylosing spondylitis
  • Tendonitis and bursitis

How to Take It

Follow your prescription or the product leaflet and ask a pharmacist or prescriber if you are unsure. This page does not provide an adult dosing schedule. Do not take naproxen for longer than directed without medical advice.

Side Effects

  • Stomach upset, indigestion, or heartburn
  • Nausea
  • Headache
  • Dizziness
  • Drowsiness
  • Skin rash
  • In rare cases, stomach ulcers or bleeding

Who Should Avoid Naproxen?

Naproxen is not suitable for everyone. People with stomach ulcers, kidney or liver problems, heart disease, or high blood pressure should use naproxen with caution or avoid it altogether. It is also not recommended during pregnancy, especially in the third trimester. Children under 16 should not take naproxen unless prescribed by a doctor.

Naproxen vs Ibuprofen

Naproxen and ibuprofen are both NSAIDs. Which is suitable depends on your health, other medicines and the reason for treatment. Do not take them together. Ask a pharmacist or prescriber rather than assuming one is milder or safer for you.

/library/naproxen-side-effects.title: Naproxen Side Effects: Common Problems and Serious Risks
/library/naproxen-side-effects.description: Naproxen side effects can include stomach pain, nausea and dizziness. Learn about serious risks, warning symptoms and when to seek medical help.
/library/naproxen-side-effects.question: Naproxen Side Effects: Common Problems and Serious Risks
/library/naproxen-side-effects.answer: Naproxen side effects can include stomach pain, nausea, dizziness and tiredness. More serious problems include stomach bleeding, kidney problems and severe allergic reactions. If you think you are having a serious side effect, seek urgent medical advice. Call 999 for severe breathing difficulty or swelling of the tongue or throat.
/library/naproxen-side-effects.bodyHtml:
Overview

Naproxen is well-tolerated by many people, but like all NSAIDs, it can cause side effects. The risk of side effects increases with higher doses and longer duration of use. This guide covers the most important side effects to be aware of.

Common Side Effects (affect more than 1 in 100 people)

  • Indigestion and heartburn
  • Stomach pain or discomfort
  • Nausea
  • Constipation or diarrhoea
  • Headache
  • Dizziness
  • Drowsiness

Serious Side Effects (seek medical advice promptly)

  • Stomach ulcer — symptoms include persistent stomach pain, indigestion that doesn't improve, and loss of appetite
  • Gastrointestinal bleeding — dark, tarry, or bloody stools; vomiting blood (coffee-ground appearance) — seek emergency help immediately
  • Allergic reaction — rash, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, difficulty breathing — seek emergency help
  • Kidney problems — reduced urine output, swollen ankles, unusual tiredness
  • Liver problems — yellowing of skin or eyes (jaundice)
  • Heart attack or stroke symptoms — chest pain, sudden severe headache, facial drooping, arm weakness — call 999

How to Reduce Side Effect Risk

  • Always take with food or milk
  • Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time
  • Take a stomach-protecting medicine (PPI) if prescribed
  • Avoid alcohol
  • Stay hydrated
  • Inform your doctor of all other medications

/library/what-is-gout.title: What Is Gout? Symptoms, Diagnosis and Treatment
/library/what-is-gout.description: What is gout? Learn how urate crystals cause joint inflammation, the symptoms, how gout is diagnosed and treatments for flares and long-term control.
/library/what-is-gout.question: What is gout?
/library/what-is-gout.answer: Gout is a type of inflammatory arthritis caused by urate crystals in and around a joint. It often causes sudden, severe pain and swelling, commonly in the big toe but also in other joints. A painful, swollen joint can also be an infection, so do not diagnose gout yourself. Treatment can control flares and lower urate to prevent future problems.
/library/what-is-gout.bodyHtml:
Overview

Gout is a form of inflammatory arthritis that develops when there is too much uric acid in the blood (hyperuricaemia). Uric acid is produced when the body breaks down purines — substances found naturally in the body and in many foods. When uric acid levels are too high, it can crystallise and deposit in joints as needle-like monosodium urate crystals, triggering intense inflammation and pain. Gout is more common in men and becomes increasingly common with age. It affects around 2.5% of the UK population.

Why Does Uric Acid Build Up?

Uric acid levels rise either because the body produces too much of it, or the kidneys do not excrete enough. Several factors contribute:

  • Diet — high intake of red meat, organ meats, shellfish, alcohol, and sugary drinks
  • Obesity
  • Kidney disease — reduced kidney function means less uric acid is excreted
  • Genetic factors
  • Certain medications — diuretics (water tablets), low-dose aspirin, ciclosporin
  • Dehydration

Stages of Gout

  • Asymptomatic hyperuricaemia — high uric acid but no symptoms yet
  • Acute gout — sudden, severe joint attacks
  • Intercritical gout — periods between attacks with no symptoms
  • Chronic tophaceous gout — persistent gout with visible deposits (tophi) if untreated

Treatment Goals

The two main goals of gout treatment are: (1) treating acute attacks promptly with NSAIDs, colchicine, or corticosteroids, and (2) preventing future attacks and lowering uric acid levels in the long term with medications like allopurinol or febuxostat, combined with lifestyle changes.
